description.narrative: CMI!’s vision is a gender-equal and just world where all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people enjoy their rights fully and live to their full potential. Our role in bringing about this vision is to support movements to be resilient and leverage their power to create change from local to global and from global to local, thereby engendering systemic and sustainable change at all levels.

In order for feminist civil society movements to be strong and autonomous39 (an ambitious achievement in itself), self-led WHRDs and WROs go through three intermediate steps - resulting in CMI!’s output (see section 4 and Annex 1, our Results Framework). WHRDs and WROs must be: RESOURCED with the knowledge, resources, and skills for impact, including for L&A. COORDINATED to be able to organise together to articulate priorities and take collective action, including amplifying voices through alliances between structurally excluded movements, linking with more mainstream movements where possible. RESILIENT by having resources, networks, strength and holistic security in place to sustain their work including in the face of backlash and closing civic space, build broader support bases, and expand their work.

Our five-year strategic objective is: political actors, societal actors and donors at local, national, regional and global levels take action to recognise, protect and fulfil the human rights of all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people as a result of strong and autonomous feminist movements holding them to account.

They continue to push for the ""Local Act for the Welfare of Sex Workers"".SMS focused on resisting policies that would limit the rights and safety of sex workers. SMS actively engaged with local authorities like the political leaders and lawmakers to resist any potential legislation like the ITPA that could criminalize sex workers or make their lives more vulnerable to violence and exploitation. Through public awareness campaigns and meeting with policymakers, SMS ensured that the voices of the sex worker community were heard, advocating for protective laws and rejecting proposals that would marginalize or harm them further.SMS's collaborations with other rights-based organizations further strengthened their position, as they presented unified demands for inclusive and protective policies. "APNSW developed a 3 days training packages on human rights, SRHR and social protection issues. Each county 15 – 20 community leaders received this training in 6 countries (Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Vietnam and Indonesia). APNSW conducted a regional training in Bangkok with 16 sex worker leaders from four countries (Bangladesh, Laos, Myanmar, and Indonesia) for two days. This training was focused on the anti-violence project aimed at promoting and protecting the human rights of sex workers. APNSW held a Regional Advocacy meeting with stakeholders and sex workers to implement CEDAW in 4 countrie (Nepal, Vietnam, Mongolia and Laos). A total of 20 people attended with representatives from the sex workers communities, Government and CSOs. An anonymous organisation created and defended the following spaces: Provided legal awareness training to 60 sex workers. This allowed sex workers in the community have more opportunities to speak out against harassment, violence, and stigmatisation and to encourage allies to prevent violence. An anonymous organisation reported organising a training on sexual and reproductive health rights (SRHR) was for 30 sex workers including access to comprehensive services in order to create advocactes for those denied funding for HIV and health care. An anonymous organistion reported organising two events with government agencies, CBOs, netowrks and allianceswwhere held in which sex workers used their adovacy skills to provide educational content to stakeholders.Celebrations where held by an anonymous organisation to honor key dates within the sex worker movement as well as 16 days against GBV along with other state level NGOs.An anonymous organisation provided a training workshop with 30 leaders from 10 CBOs to strengthen community systems including engaging with governmental departments and stakeholders. An anonymous organisaton ment with labour and domestic workers, farm workers, and other similarly situated groups to sensitise them to sex work as work and resulted in a noticeable change in attitude of the groups.

"During 2022 APNSW reported working to end violence against sex workers, stigma, and discriminations. One of their core activities is toend violence against sex workers, advocating within CEDAW structures at national level to guarantee meaningful participation of sex workers community. APNSW provided technical support in Lao during this period, they reported that following engagement by the member organisation in the country, the government has shifeted its lanugage around stigma and descrijination against sex workers. The member, WLIC explained, “Now we are always talking about sex workers rights, violence, stigma and discrimination. The Government and stakeholders often accept those.”An anonymous organisation focused on community empowerment and did not report blocking, adopting or improving laws as a strategy. However, they did launch a community led training to address police violence and harassment including learning how to identify and monitor the behaviors in order to develop an action plan to confront and improve these outcomes.An anonymous organisation reported engaging in advocacy to resist a variety of laws and policies including a national anti-trafficking law. MSS engaged in a long term strategy of training peer mobilisers to reach into different districts to gather evidence, document and monitor incidents of violence in order to advocate for improved protection of female sex workers facing human rights violations.MSS trainings on human rights created pressure groups and allies to influence police and security personnel not to arrest female sex workes at hotels and public places as well as support legal reform to laws criminalising sex work. This included strategy sessions to develop specfic policies. Nijgadh Mahila Samuha (NMS) conducted 4 orientations with concerned agencies & local level Government partners regarding the situations & issues of sex workers within our catchment area. - Sex workers have gained confidence in using their skills and knowledge in advocacy, in effectively representing sex workers in decision-making forums, and in building partnerships based on which Sex workers’ human rights are promoted and protected.- The local municipality has designed some activities in this year's annual planning for skill-based in-come-generating activities for vulnerable groups including hotel & cabin/bar girls.- Previously journalists were negative towards sex work & sex workers but after the orientation, they always call us and ask what the issue is, before writing anything in local/National media. - Local agencies & local government (Municipality) invite Nijgadh Mahila Samuha (NMS) in like-minded programs related to women's health, GBV (gender-based violence), and SRH to share our experiences, so Sex worker groups are now able to openly put their voices in local municipality & police office."
